column2: Abstract: Sheil-Small asked whether every self-inversive P maps D onto a domain containing a disc of radius A; the answer is yes (l.13-15); Table l.69-70 "(in particular every self-inversive P)"; l.60-61 "We answer the question in the affirmative"; l.86-87

Abstract: every non-constant P whose coefficients have the same moduli when read in reverse order maps D onto a DOMAIN containing an open disc of radius A (l.15-16; Table l.69-70; l.84-86) — thm_4_1 at n = deg P

Abstract: the class contains both the self-inversive P (zeros symmetric w.r.t. the circle) and the P whose zeros, with multiplicity, are symmetric under reciprocals (the literal reading), so the theorem answers the question under either reading (l.16-19; l.86; l.106-110; Figure 1 caption l.97-98)
Abstract l.19-20 and l.86-87, 102, 110-111, 435: the radius A cannot be increased; the disc must be taken open (1+z^n: A=1, P(D)=D(1,1))
Abstract: all zeros on the circle -> the largest disc in the image has radius exactly M/2 (l.20-21; Table l.73-74; l.88-90)
Abstract: for these polynomials the question is equivalent to asking whether every coefficient has modulus at most M/2 (l.21-22); Table l.73-74 "equivalent to M >= 2A"
Intro: P*(z) = z^n conj P(1/conj z) = sum conj(a_{n-k}) z^k (l.43; also l.163)
Intro: for P(0) != 0, self-inversive iff the zeros are symmetric w.r.t. the circle, with multiplicities (l.45-47)
Intro: every self-inversive polynomial satisfies lambda = 1 after multiplication by a suitable constant of modulus 1 (l.48-49)
Intro: 1+3iz+z^2 satisfies a_{n-k} = +-a_k but is not self-inversive (l.107-108)
Intro and Table: de Bruijn's covering theorem (Lemma 3.2 is the form we use) at a point of maximum modulus, where zeta P'(zeta) = (n/2) P(zeta), gives the disc of radius M/2 (l.75-76, 121-122)
Intro: "In Theorem 3.1, that no open disc of radius larger than M/2 lies in P(D) is elementary" (no cited input) (l.125)

Intro: the circle case of the question can be assembled from results in print (l.125-126); Figure 1 caption: when all zeros lie on the unit circle, a disc of radius A follows from results in print: M >= 2A with de Bruijn's theorem (l.100-101)

Intro: by Theorem 3.1, a positive answer for self-inversive polynomials implies the inequality M >= 2A of OR74, SS74, Kr79 for polynomials with all zeros on the unit circle (l.127-129; the row assumes the covering only for zeros on the circle, a subclass, so it is at least as strong)
Intro: for self-inversive P the disc of radius M/2 still exists (Proposition 3.3), but M/2 may be smaller than A: 1+4z+z^2 has M/2 = 3, A = 4 (l.129-131)

Intro, the idea of the proof (l.134-146): zero-free H has |zH'| <= |nH - zH'| on the circle; with (H(z) conj H(eta) - H*(z) conj H*(eta))/(1 - z conj eta) = sum K_ij z^i conj(eta)^j, the Hermitian form of Schur and Cohn, given by the matrix (K_ij), is PSD and its entries are explicit in the coefficients of H (Lemma 2.2); in the proof of Theorem 3.1 the first fact at a maximum point places every omitted value at distance >= M/2 from P(zeta)/2; for Theorem 4.1, P of degree at most n, not constant (Theorem 4.1's hypothesis), with |a_k| = |a_{n-k}|: a_0 = 0: every omitted w != 0, a 2x2 minor of (K_ij) gives |w| >= A, D(0,A) in P(D); normalize a_0 = a_n = 1; the diagonal entries K_jj all equal |1-w|^2-1 >= 0, so |1-w| >= 1, D(1,1) in P(D) (every A) and A = 1 is settled; A > 1: E = a_{n-j}/conj(a_j), |E| = 1, the minor on the indices 0 and j gives |w-(1+E)| >= A unless w = 1-E, so D(1+E,A) minus w_* is taken; w_* indeed omitted -> P - w_* has all zeros on the circle and the same A (then Theorem 3.1 with M >= 2A applies)
Figure 1: the two symmetry classes lie in the class (eq:mirror); the polynomials with all zeros on the unit circle are self-inversive (caption l.97-99)

Figure 1, right: Theorem 4.1 gives a disc of radius A for every non-constant member of the class; Theorem 3.1 the exact largest radius M/2 when all zeros lie on the unit circle (l.101-102); the figure's words "Yes. Theorem 4.1: a disc of radius A for every non-constant P with |a_k|=|a_{n-k}|" restate Theorem 4.1

Figure 1: 1+z+5z^2+z^3+z^4 is self-inversive, A = 5, its zeros lie off the unit circle, and P(D) contains a disc of radius A = 5 (caption l.96-97; the figure's words "as here", "with largest coefficient A=5", "disc of radius A" and "A=5" on the radius)
Section 2: H* for deg H <= n; (H*)* = H; |H*| = |H| on the circle (l.162-164)
Lemma 2.1: in both cases |a_k| = |a_{n-k}| (l.175)
Lemma 2.1: all zeros on the circle -> self-inversive (l.175-176, proof l.187)
Before Lemma 2.2 (l.190): part (a) says, on |z| = 1, |H'(z)| <= |(H*)'(z)| (H of degree <= n with no zero in D)
Lemma 2.2, eq. (eq:factor) (l.195-199)
Lemma 2.2(a) (l.202); equality at a zero on the circle (l.230)
Lemma 2.2(b): K(z,eta) is a polynomial in z, conj eta with PSD coefficient matrix (l.203-208); eq. (eq:one-factor) (l.232-235)
Lemma 2.2(c), eq. (eq:entries) (l.209-213)
Lemma 3.2 (l.269-272): a single boundary point forces a whole disc into the image (l.264), also for degree less than n (l.267)
Proposition 3.3 with "in particular F'(zeta) != 0" (l.280-283, 292-293)
Theorem 3.4 [Kr79, Kr80, OR74, SS74] (l.308-311) — the ONE cited result (Sheil.Cited.coef_half_max)

Note after Theorem 3.4 (l.314-319): m = n/2; P* = lambda P, |lambda| = 1 (Lemma 2.1); Q(theta) = e^{-im theta} P(e^{i theta}) has conj Q = lambda Q; T = cQ is real when c^2 = lambda; T is a real trigonometric polynomial of exact degree m (top coefficient c a_n != 0) whose 2m zeros in a period are all real (stated through the zeros of P: 2m with multiplicity, T = 0 iff P(e^{i theta}) = 0, every zero real, a period's zeros one-to-one with P's); max |T| = M(P); constant term t_0 = c a_{n/2}; "the case k = n/2 says that ... |t_0| <= (1/2) max|T|" (the middle case iff |c a_m| <= sup|T|/2; the bound itself is T34)
Corollary 3.5 (l.321-323)
Theorem 4.1, Case 2, the normalization; it multiplies every radius and A by 1/|a_0| and preserves (eq:mirror) (l.355-357)
Theorem 4.1, Case 2: constant diagonal d = |1-w|^2-1, d >= 0 i.e. |w-1| >= 1 for every omitted w, A = 1 gives D(1,1) (l.359-365)
Theorem 4.1, eq. (eq:minor) (l.367-372)
Theorem 4.1, eq. (eq:punctured): every omitted value other than w_* = 1-E lies outside D(1+E,A) (l.373-378)
Theorem 4.1, w_* omitted: S = P - w_* has all zeros on the circle, A(S) = A, P(D) = S(D) + w_* (l.380-384; l.380 "if w_* in P(D) ... we are done")
Remark 4.2: |w_* - (1+E)| = 2, so w_* is in D(1+E,A) only when A > 2, i.e. A > 2|a_0| before the normalization (l.388-389)
Remark 4.2: Theorem 3.4 is needed only when A > 2|a_0| and w_* is omitted; otherwise (eq:punctured) already gives D(1+E,A) in P(D) (l.389-390)
Remark 4.2: if A is attained at j != n/2, then A(S) = |a_j| with j != n/2, and [OR74, Thm 3] or [SS74, Thm 3] suffices (l.391-392)
Remark 4.2: the middle case of Theorem 3.4 is used only when n is even, |a_{n/2}| is strictly larger than every other |a_k| and than 2|a_0|, and w_* is omitted (l.392-393)
Remark 4.2: the middle case cannot be bypassed — for zeros on the circle Theorem 4.1 is equivalent to Theorem 3.4, so every proof of Theorem 4.1 also proves the middle case (l.393-395)
Section 5 opener (l.400-401), Figure 1 caption l.102, l.111-112 and l.438: the radius A in Theorem 4.1 cannot be increased, and this remains true when A is large compared with |a_0|
Figure 2, left: (1+z)^2, the cardioid rho = 2+2cos psi bounds P(D); zeros on the circle; M = 4, A = 2; the largest disc is D(2,2), radius M/2 = A (caption l.426-428, label l.412, picture l.405-413)

Figure 2, right: 1+4z+z^2, the limacon rho = 4+2cos psi bounds P(D); strip -2 < Re w < 6; D(2,4) inside, largest radius A = 4; the grey disc D(3,3), of radius M/2 (M = 6), inside; label "A = 4, M = 6" (caption l.428-430, label l.424, picture l.415-425)
Example 5.1: 1+z^n, A = 1, P(D) = D(1,1), no open disc of radius > 1, no closed disc of radius 1 (l.433-436)

Example 5.2: 1+a z^m+z^{2m}, a >= 4: circle formula, Re P, derivative a+4x >= 0, range [2-a,2+a], strip of width 2a, radius <= a = A; E = 1, w_* = 0 is taken (P has a zero in D), the disc of the proof is D(2,a) (l.440-451)
